items.title: Bullion may remain under pressure as markets track US-Iran war, inflation
items.summary: The focus will be on inflation prints from China, the US, Germany, Japan and India. Investors will also closely track speeches by Federal Reserve officials and US employment data

events.article_text:
On the Multi Commodity Exchange, gold futures for December delivery gained ₹3,682, or nearly 3 per cent, over the past week to close at ₹1.42 lakh per 10 grams | Image: Bloomberg

Bullion prices are likely to remain under pressure next week as investors track developments in the US-Iran conflict, movements in crude oil prices and inflation data for cues on the outlook for interest rates, analysts said.

The focus will be on inflation prints from China, the US, Germany, Japan and India. Investors will also closely track speeches by Federal Reserve officials and US employment data.

Chinese economic indicators will be important for industrial metals, they added.

Geopolitical developments will remain a key driver after US President Donald Trump confirmed fresh military strikes on Iran, while claiming that Washington had made "a lot of progress" in negotiations with Tehran, adding another layer of uncertainty.

The domestic commodities market will remain closed during the morning session on Tuesday due to Diwali-Balipratipada.

"Gold and silver's momentum remains down as investors will focus on the inflation data from China, the US, Germany, Japan, India, etc along with some Fed officials' commentary," said Pranav Mer, Senior Vice President, EBG - Commodity & Currency Research, JM Financial Services Ltd.

He said investors would also track progress in peace negotiations between the US and Iran to end the war, as well as Russia-Ukraine peace talks.

In international markets, Comex gold futures for December delivery advanced $176, or 4.5 per cent, during the week to close at $4,074.9 per ounce. Silver gained $2.6, or 5.4 per cent, to settle at $51.94 per ounce.

Mer said bullion prices initially faced pressure from stronger-than-expected US nonfarm payroll data and improving consumer sentiment, which lifted the dollar and Treasury yields.

"However, prices ended with a strong weekly gain of more than 4 per cent in global markets, following a sharp rally mid-week after the US midterm election outcome that showed Democrats sweeping wins in both the Senate and the House over the Republicans," he added.

Analysts said precious metals recovered during the week on bargain buying at lower levels and short-covering, although gains were capped by a correction in industrial metals, particularly copper.

The rally was also supported by safe-haven demand following a decline in AI, data centre and technology stocks in global markets, particularly in the US.

However, bullion futures came under selling pressure on Friday, with gold and silver closing around $4,074 and $52 per ounce, respectively, Mer said.

In the domestic market, prices could witness moderate fluctuations, with global cues, currency movements, inflation trends and festive demand around Diwali likely to influence trading.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

analysis.tldr: Global gold prices are swinging due to the US-Iran conflict, US elections, and inflation data, which will directly affect festive gold shopping costs in India.
the_story: On the Multi Commodity Exchange, December gold futures gained ₹3,682 to close at ₹1.42 lakh per 10 grams over the past week.
US President Donald Trump confirmed fresh military strikes on Iran while mentioning progress in negotiations.
Global gold futures on Comex rose $176 to $4,074.9 per ounce, and silver rose to $51.94 per ounce over the week.
Prices rose due to safe-haven demand after tech and AI stocks dropped, bargain buying, and the US midterm election outcome where Democrats won the Senate and House.
Prices faced early pressure and Friday selling due to strong US employment data that lifted the US dollar and Treasury yields (interest paid by the US government).
analysis.what_happened: Gold and silver prices rose globally and in India over the past week, driven by a mix of political uncertainty from US-Iran tensions, US election results, and a drop in tech stocks that pushed investors to seek safe assets. However, strong US job market data and rising US Treasury yields caused temporary selling pressure on gold.
analysis.analogy: It is like a bustling local market where people rush to buy safety-deposit lockers when they hear shouting outside, but momentarily pause buying whenever the local bank announces it is paying higher interest on cash savings.
why_it_matters_india: Global gold prices rise due to safe-haven buying during wars and political shifts.
Higher global gold prices translate to higher domestic prices on the Multi Commodity Exchange.
Festive demand around Diwali in India interacts with these global prices to influence local retail buying.
Indian consumers face costlier precious metals for gifting and festive purchases.

impacts.rationale: Global safe-haven demand and festive demand are keeping domestic futures elevated, making jewelry and bullion purchases more expensive for households.
Global silver tracking safe-haven flows has risen, increasing costs for local retail buyers.

watch_next: Upcoming inflation data prints from the US, India, China, Germany, and Japan
Developments in the US-Iran conflict and peace negotiations
Speeches by Federal Reserve officials regarding interest rate outlooks
analysis.caveats: Unexpected shifts in US employment numbers or sudden diplomatic breakthroughs in the US-Iran conflict could quickly reverse bullion price trends.

events.headline: Iran war: IOC to buy crude, LPG carriers as Strait of Hormuz disruptions drive freight costs

items.title: Iran war: IOC to buy crude, LPG carriers as Strait of Hormuz disruptions drive freight costs
items.summary: Indian Oil Corporation plans to buy crude and LPG carriers and explore shipbuilding in India as Strait of Hormuz disruptions drive up freight costs. The move complements efforts to diversify crude supplies, increase inventories and strengthen resilience across its energy supply chain.

events.article_text:
State-owned Indian Oil Corporation plans to acquire crude oil and liquefied petroleum gas carriers of its own as disruptions to shipping around the Strait of Hormuz and soaring freight costs prompt India's largest oil refiner to strengthen control over its energy supply chain.

The company's board has already approved the purchase of a few vessels, and tenders were issued several months ago, Director of Finance Anuj Jain said during its second-quarter earnings call.

"The country needs oil sector companies to focus more on the shipping area now," Jain said, adding that IOC was also exploring the possibility of building ships in India under the government's Make in India initiative.

The move marks a potential shift in the company's shipping strategy, which has traditionally relied on a mix of time-charter and voyage-chartered vessels. IOC is now examining three approaches: optimising existing charter arrangements, owning ships and supporting domestic shipbuilding.

The importance of securing shipping capacity has increased as geopolitical tensions in West Asia disrupt commercial movement near the Strait of Hormuz, pushing up freight rates and war-risk insurance costs.

IOC currently has three crude oil vessels and nine LPG vessels on time charter. These arrangements have provided significant cost savings during the current crisis, Jain said.

The company's time-chartered crude carriers cost around USD 2-2.50 per barrel, compared to spot-market rates of as much as USD 8-10 per barrel.

LPG freight rates, which would normally be around USD 40 per tonne, have risen to USD 160-180 per tonne in the spot market, he said.

The shipping strategy is part of a broader effort to diversify crude procurement and reduce exposure to supply disruptions. IOC sourced 55 per cent of its crude requirements from Russia during the first half of the current financial year, while Middle Eastern supplies accounted for 24 per cent, Jain said.

Africa contributed about 10 per cent, Brazil 7 per cent, the United States 2-5 per cent and Venezuela 3-4 per cent.

The company has also substantially increased its reliance on spot purchases. Spot imports accounted for about 87 per cent of crude sourcing in the first half of FY27, compared to around 50 per cent in the previous financial year.

Jain said the company had been able to negotiate discounts against benchmark prices even as global crude markets remained volatile. The premium or discount paid over benchmark crude during the September quarter ranged from a discount of USD 5 per barrel to a premium of USD 12 per barrel, compared to a range of zero to USD 18 per barrel in the preceding quarter.

IOC has continued to buy Russian crude at what it described as optimal prices and has also been processing Venezuelan crude.

The company's procurement diversification comes against the backdrop of a sharp rise in oil prices following the escalation of US-Iran hostilities towards the end of February.

Indian basket crude, which averaged around USD 65-70 per barrel in February, remained above USD 100 for much of the first quarter and averaged about USD 120 per barrel in October, Jain said.

Despite the supply-chain disruptions, IOC said it had maintained refinery operations at optimal levels and increased crude inventories to about 39 days, from its usual 33-35 days. It was also holding 20 days of LPG inventory and 23-25 days of petrol and diesel stocks.

IOC reported a net profit of ₹21,630 crore in the September quarter, compared with a loss of ₹2,661 crore in the preceding quarter and a profit of ₹7,610 crore in the year-earlier period. The company said inventory gains and improved performance across several businesses contributed to its profitability.

It recorded a gross refining margin of USD 18.52 per barrel, excluding the impact of the special additional excise duty, and an inventory gain of USD 6,948 crore during the quarter.

Jain cautioned that geopolitical developments remained a key source of uncertainty for the company, particularly because of their impact on crude procurement, freight and marketing margins.

The proposed vessel purchases and domestic shipbuilding initiative reflect a wider effort by Indian oil companies to strengthen logistics resilience as India remains heavily dependent on imported crude and overseas shipping routes.

analysis.tldr: Rising shipping costs due to Middle East conflicts mean Indian oil companies may spend more to bring fuel home, which could eventually make filling up your vehicle costlier.
the_story: State-owned Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) plans to buy its own crude oil and LPG (liquefied petroleum gas) carriers to control its energy supply chain.
Geopolitical tensions near the Strait of Hormuz have disrupted shipping, pushing spot freight rates for crude up to USD 8-10 per barrel and LPG rates to USD 160-180 per tonne.
IOC sourced 55% of its crude from Russia and 24% from the Middle East in the first half of the financial year, while increasing spot purchases to 87%.
analysis.what_happened: IOC decided to buy its own ships and explore domestic shipbuilding because conflicts near the Strait of Hormuz have pushed up the cost of renting transport ships and war-risk insurance. At the same time, oil prices surged due to US-Iran hostilities, with Indian basket crude averaging around USD 120 per barrel in October.
analysis.analogy: It is like a grocery shop owner who usually rents delivery vans getting tired of soaring rental prices during a fuel shortage, and deciding to buy their own trucks to keep delivery costs down.
why_it_matters_india: Middle East conflict causes shipping disruptions and higher freight costs -> Indian oil refiners face increased transport expenses -> Higher crude and shipping costs raise import bills -> This can ultimately pressure the rupee and domestic fuel costs.
IOC builds up larger reserves (39 days of crude inventory) to buffer against supply shocks -> This provides short-term stability to refinery operations despite external conflicts.

impacts.rationale: Higher global crude prices and soaring freight costs make importing and refining fuel more expensive, which is bad for everyday consumers at the pump.
IOC reported a strong net profit of ₹21,630 crore for the September quarter backed by inventory gains, though long-term margins remain vulnerable to geopolitical uncertainty.

watch_next: Developments around the Strait of Hormuz and shipping lane security
Global crude oil benchmark prices and Indian basket averages
analysis.caveats: If geopolitical tensions in West Asia ease quickly, shipping freight rates and war-risk insurance costs could drop faster than expected.

items.title: Oil Traders Want U.S. to Release Sanctioned Tankers as Freight Costs Soar
items.summary: Some of the world's biggest oil traders are asking Washington for permission to put sanctioned tankers back to work, as a global vessel shortage pushes oil transportation costs to extraordinary levels. Trafigura, Vitol, Mercuria and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. are negotiating with U.S. officials for licenses to purchase or lease blacklisted oil tankers, Bloomberg reported Friday, citing people familiar with the discussions. The talks involve approximately 50 vessels currently under U.S. sanctions. Treasury officials are considering approvals on…

events.article_text:
Oil Traders Want U.S. to Release Sanctioned Tankers as Freight Costs Soar

Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her…

Some of the world's biggest oil traders are asking Washington for permission to put sanctioned tankers back to work, as a global vessel shortage pushes oil transportation costs to extraordinary levels.

Trafigura, Vitol, Mercuria and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. are negotiating with U.S. officials for licenses to purchase or lease blacklisted oil tankers, Bloomberg reported Friday, citing people familiar with the discussions.

The talks involve approximately 50 vessels currently under U.S. sanctions. Treasury officials are considering approvals on a case-by-case basis, although no decisions have been finalized.

The proposal comes after months of shipping disruptions stemming from the Iran war, which has forced tankers onto longer routes, increased insurance costs, and tied up vessels in inefficient transfers around the Strait of Hormuz.

The cost of chartering a supertanker from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China reached nearly $80 million in October, roughly ten times the average rate before the conflict.

Valero estimated last month that shipping U.S. crude to Asia had reached $30 to $35 per barrel, compared with approximately $5 a year earlier.

Those costs have consequences. Asian orders for U.S. crude for November delivery fell roughly 50% in October, potentially pushing shipments to their lowest level in seven years.

Adding sanctioned vessels could relieve some of that pressure.

U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said last month that Washington was exploring arrangements allowing investors to acquire and refurbish blacklisted tankers for transporting legitimate oil cargoes.

As of November 4, U.S. sanctions covered 1,568 ships, including 462 crude tankers, according to Treasury data compiled by Bloomberg.

But the potential benefit depends heavily on which vessels receive approval. Restoring previously idled tankers would add actual shipping capacity. Simply legalizing vessels already transporting sanctioned oil would do considerably less to ease the shortage.

Many blacklisted tankers are also aging vessels requiring repairs, inspections and insurance before entering conventional commercial service, and U.S. authorization would not automatically remove restrictions imposed by the European Union or Britain.

analysis.tldr: Soaring global shipping costs make imported crude oil pricier, which can push up domestic fuel and inflation rates in India.
the_story: Global oil traders like Trafigura, Vitol, Mercuria, and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. are asking U.S. officials for licenses to use about 50 blacklisted or sanctioned oil tankers.

Shipping disruptions from the Iran war forced tankers onto longer routes and tied up vessels, pushing the cost of chartering a supertanker from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China to nearly $80 million in October (ten times the normal rate before the conflict).
Shipping U.S. crude to Asia rose to $30–$35 per barrel compared to about $5 a year earlier, causing Asian orders for U.S. crude for November delivery to drop roughly 50% in October.
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said last month that Washington is exploring letting investors acquire and fix up blacklisted tankers to carry legitimate oil.

U.S. Treasury data shows sanctions covered 1,568 ships (including 462 crude tankers) as of November 4, and many aging ships need repairs and insurance before they can safely return to commercial service.
analysis.what_happened: Global oil traders are asking the U.S. government for special permission to use roughly 50 sanctioned oil tankers because a severe shortage of ships has sent transportation costs soaring. This shortage was caused by months of shipping disruptions from the Iran war, which forced tankers onto longer routes and hiked insurance costs.
analysis.analogy: It is like a major delivery truck strike that forces remaining delivery vans to take much longer detours, causing delivery fees for goods to shoot through the roof.
why_it_matters_india: High global shipping and transport costs make buying and moving crude oil more expensive worldwide.
Since India imports a vast majority of its crude oil, higher transport and oil costs increase the total import bill.
A higher oil import bill puts upward pressure on domestic retail fuel prices and general inflation (the rate at which prices rise).
Rising inflation and import costs can weaken the rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars), which impacts broader financial markets.

impacts.rationale: Higher global shipping costs for oil can eventually feed into pricier domestic fuel, which is generally bad for everyday household budgets.
Costlier fuel and transport drive up the price of goods and services across the economy, reducing consumer purchasing power.
A higher oil import bill means India needs more U.S. dollars to buy energy, which tends to weaken the local currency and make imports costlier.

watch_next: Whether the U.S. government actually grants licenses to release the sanctioned tankers
Changes in global freight rates for oil tankers
analysis.caveats: If the U.S. quickly approves licenses for the blocked tankers, shipping bottlenecks could ease and bring transport costs down faster than expected.

events.headline: US Government Announces Fresh Sanctions Against Cambodia-based Scam Network

items.title: US Government Announces Fresh Sanctions Against Cambodia-based Scam Network
items.summary: The U.S. Treasury Department says that actors linked to Prince Group targeted victims across with world via "sophisticated cyber-enabled fraud schemes."

events.article_text:
The United States yesterday announced a new tranche of sanctions against Cambodia’s Prince Holding Group, which it has accused of running a region-wide network of online scamming centers.

In a statement, the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) said that it had sanctioned an additional four individuals and 41 entities “that support the business network of Prince Group Transnational Criminal Organization.”

“Prince Group TCO-affiliated actors have targeted victims in the United States and around the world through sophisticated cyber-enabled fraud schemes, including digital asset investment scams, romance scams, and other online financial fraud,” it stated. “Today’s action further targets the corporate and financial infrastructure that has enabled Prince Group TCO leaders to conceal assets, evade prior sanctions, and maintain access to the international financial system.” According to U.S. government estimates, such scams cost U.S. citizens at least $10 billion in 2024.

Treasury’s action comes after an operation in October of 2025, in which OFAC announced sanctions on 146 individuals and entities connected to Prince Holding Group, including its 38-year-old chairman Chen Zhi. It designated the group a “transnational criminal organization,” alleging its involvement in cyberfraud, human trafficking, and money laundering.

The sanctions were part of what Treasury described as the “largest action ever” to disrupt Southeast Asia’s scamming operations, which are run predominantly by Chinese criminal syndicates and have relied on a huge number of trafficked workers from across the globe. In a parallel announcement, federal prosecutors in the U.S. also unsealed an indictment charging Chen with wire fraud and money laundering. They accused him of “the construction, operation, and management of scam compounds reliant on human trafficking and modern-day slavery” and of authorizing bribes to foreign officials to protect his business interests.

Chen allegedly built his empire with the benefit of connections at the highest echelon of Cambodian politics. He served as an advisor to both former Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Sen and his son and successor Hun Manet, and was the recipient of the neak oknha title, one of the country’s highest honorifics. The sanctions, as well as growing pressure from Chinese authorities, in January prompted the Cambodian government to deport Chen to China, where he now faces a host of criminal charges, including some that carry the death penalty.

In June of this year, OFAC sanctioned an additional nine individuals and 26 entities linked to Prince Group, “including TCO leadership, investors in scam compounds, and front companies.”

According to OFAC, the individuals and entities named in the latest round of sanctions “have helped sustain Prince Group TCO’s illicit global operations after the October 2025 and June 2026 designations by managing offshore corporate structures, concealing beneficial ownership, facilitating commercial activities, and providing administrative and financial services to senior Prince Group TCO executives.”

They include Qiu Yong, whom Treasury described as a “key” member of the Prince network who controls multiple companies in Hong Kong and the British Virgin Islands, and who served as an employee of a company controlled by Chen Zhi, and his personal assistant Zhao Mengyao. Also listed were Cambodian nationals He Yujing and Visal Pang, who were sanctioned for holding property for, or co-directing companies with, Prince Group TCO executive Chen Bo, who was among those sanctioned in June.

More than 200 individuals and entities have now been sanctioned by the U.S. government, a testament to the intricacy of the networks established in order to conceal Prince Group’s ill-gotten profits. This also suggests that American investigators will be unraveling Chen’s tangled web for some time to come.

analysis.tldr: This news has virtually no direct impact on your daily expenses, loans, or the Indian stock market.
the_story: The U.S. Treasury Department announced a new round of sanctions against Cambodia’s Prince Holding Group, targeting four individuals and 41 entities.
The U.S. government states these groups run cyber-enabled fraud schemes like digital asset investment scams and romance scams, costing U.S. citizens at least $10 billion in 2024.
The group's chairman, Chen Zhi, was previously sanctioned, deported to China in January, and hit with U.S. federal indictments for wire fraud, money laundering, and human trafficking.
analysis.what_happened: The U.S. government placed financial penalties and bans on companies and people helping a Cambodia-based scam network called Prince Holding Group. This happened because U.S. authorities are trying to shut down a massive international cybercrime network that tricks people out of money and uses human trafficking.
analysis.analogy: It is like the police freezing the bank accounts of a whole network of front companies that a master criminal set up to hide money stolen from scams.
why_it_matters_india: The U.S. targets a Cambodia-based cybercrime network ->
The network used complex offshore corporate structures and digital assets to hide money ->
The action focuses strictly on U.S. victims, American financial systems, and specific individuals in Southeast Asia ->
There is no direct connection to Indian companies, the rupee, Indian inflation, or local stock markets.

impacts.rationale: Global crime crackdowns rarely affect broad Indian stock prices because local companies have no business links to these specific scam networks.
Sanctions on a Southeast Asian crime group do not alter global currency flows or demand for the US dollar in India.

watch_next: Further actions by U.S. or international law enforcement against transnational cybercrime rings
analysis.caveats: This is entirely an international law enforcement matter focused on U.S. financial systems and Southeast Asian crime syndicates, with no direct transmission channel to Indian financial markets.

events.headline: The US is in a bind: Arun Singh

items.title: The US is in a bind: Arun Singh
items.summary: The former India Ambassador to the US discusses the Republican setback in the recent US midterm elections, shifting public opinion, the Iran war’s impact on US power and the challenges facing India-US relations.

events.article_text:
Published : Nov 07, 2026 23:07 IST - 1 MIN READ

In this episode of SpeakEasy with Amit Baruah, former Indian Ambassador to the United States Arun Singh discusses the political implications of the 2026 US midterm elections and their impact on American foreign policy. With the Democrats making significant gains and voters turning against Donald Trump’s policies, Singh assesses what the results mean for the balance of power in Washington, the future of the Republican and Democratic parties, and Trump’s ability to pursue his political agenda.

The conversation examines the growing opposition to US support for Israel, the changing politics around Palestine, and the consequences of the war with Iran for American influence in West Asia. Singh also discusses the strain on US relations with its Gulf allies, the possibility of a prolonged conflict with Iran, and the changing security calculations of countries in the region.

The conversation covered significant gains by Democrats and voter backlash against Donald Trump’s policies, affecting the balance of power in Washington and Trump's political agenda.
The discussion also addressed growing US opposition regarding support for Israel, changing politics around Palestine, and the consequences of a war with Iran on American influence in West Asia.

This happens as voters push back against domestic political agendas and regional wars threaten prolonged instability.
analysis.analogy: It is like a major shopkeeper in your local market getting distracted by family arguments and local fights, causing the prices of essential goods they supply to fluctuate wildly for everyone else.

Geopolitical tension and supply-shock fears push up global crude oil and gold prices.
Because India imports most of its crude oil, costlier energy raises domestic inflation (general rise in prices) and puts pressure on the rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars).

impacts.rationale: Prolonged conflict in West Asia threatens oil supplies, driving up crude prices which is generally bad for consumers as it raises transport and goods costs.
Global geopolitical uncertainty drives investors toward safe assets like gold, making it pricier for Indian households buying jewelry or investments.
Higher global energy import bills force India to spend more dollars, which can weaken the local currency and make overall imports costlier.

Geopolitical updates regarding the conflict involving Iran and West Asia

events.headline: Interactive: Who wants what at the COP31 climate change summit

items.title: Interactive: Who wants what at the COP31 climate change summit
items.summary: Delegates will soon gather in the Turkish resort city of Antalya for UN climate negotiations, against a backdrop of war,… The post Interactive: Who wants what at the COP31 climate change summit appeared first on Carbon Brief .

items.title: As wars reshape priorities, climate cooperation faces a test at the UN Climate Summit
items.summary: When delegates from around the world gather in the Mediterranean resort town of Antalya in the Turkish Riviera for the annual, two-week United Nations climate summit (COP31) that begins on November 9, they meet at a time when wars and geopolitical rivalries are pushing governments to protect their immediate national interests even as rising temperatures, […]

events.article_text:
Delegates will soon gather in the Turkish resort city of Antalya for UN climate negotiations, against a backdrop of war, energy crisis and climate extremes.

At COP31, nations will try to find agreement on various issues, including climate finance for developing countries and a global “just transition” towards a cleaner economy.

This summit is unusual due to its joint presidency, which means that Australia is leading the negotiations while Turkey hosts the conference.

Outside the formal negotiations, Turkey is also pushing its own priorities as part of a wider “action agenda”, including electrification, oceans and “green industrialisation”.

In order to track parties’ positions on key negotiating points and wider issues at COP31, Carbon Brief has analysed around 100 documents and captured them in the interactive table below.

The first column shows the countries and UN negotiating blocs, the second shows the topics up for debate and the third indicates specific issues within those topics.

The final column indicates the positions that the parties have expressed on each topic. These range from “priority” – meaning the party is likely to be pushing the issue – to “oppose”, meaning it is likely to push against it.

This is a “living document” that will be updated over the course of COP31.

Please get in touch if you would like to offer additions by emailing [email protected].

Brief explanations of the key issues and jargon-filled language that permeate the talks can be found below the interactive table.

At COP30 in Brazil in 2025, nations agreed to establish a practical mechanism to help drive a “just transition” to a low-carbon economy.

Key aspects of this "Belém-Antalya mechanism" (BAM) – often referred to as the “just transition mechanism” (JTM) – were agreed during the June climate negotiations this year, but many details are missing and dividing lines remain between parties.

Parties have disagreed about the scope of the mechanism and whether it should be tied to the provision of finance.

Nevertheless, following progress in June within the “just transition work programme” (JTWP), civil society groups highlighted that getting the mechanism up and running is a “key expected outcome” from COP31.

Climate finance is always a highly contested issue at UN climate negotiations.

Developing countries have successfully pushed for a “work programme” on climate finance to feature on the conference agenda.

These parties see this programme as a way to pressure developed countries into providing more funding from their public coffers, specifically under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement. Some are even proposing a “burden sharing” arrangement for climate-finance provision.

This comes against a backdrop of major donors cutting their aid budgets and the Trump administration in the US pressuring multilateral development banks (MDBs) to drop their climate objectives.

Developed countries, which have traditionally been responsible for providing finance, would prefer to keep a broader focus on issues such as improving access to existing finance and broadening the range of donors. Some developing countries, such as small-island states, also support these goals.

Nations have also been discussing Article 2.1c of the Paris Agreement under the “Veredas dialogue”. This focuses on making all global “financial flows” consistent with climate action.

Countries have different views about what this involves, with developing countries again hoping to keep the focus on developed countries’ responsibilities to financially support them.

At negotiations in June, parties were unable to agree on the details of a “global goal on adaptation” (GGA), which is intended to drive climate adaptation worldwide.

Having agreed at COP30 on a list of 59 “indicators” – ways to assess progress towards the GGA – nations now need to refine these before COP32 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. This is a highly technical process that involves a taskforce working out how to use and track these indicators.

Broadly, developing countries stress the importance of finance to fund adaptation efforts, rather than simply to track progress. They also want reassurances about a pledge made last year to “triple adaptation finance”.

At the June climate negotiations, negotiators also failed to make any progress when discussing the mitigation work programme (MWP) – the only formal agenda item that concerns cutting greenhouse gas emissions.

Among other things, parties disagreed on whether the MWP should continue running over the next few years, or simply be brought to a close.

Back in 2023, the first “global stocktake” (GST) of the Paris Agreement set out the state of climate action and what needed to be done to set the world on course.

On mitigation, nations agreed to a package of measures, including “transitioning away from fossil fuels”, tripling renewable energy and “halting and reversing deforestation” by 2030.

Some of these outcomes remain contentious among certain parties, particularly large, developing countries and those with economies that rely on fossil-fuel exports.

Developing countries have persistently argued that they need more climate finance to implement the global stocktake outcomes.

Parties were meant to update their climate plans under the Paris Agreement, informed by the first global stocktake, by 2025. These plans, known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs), cover the period out to 2035.

So far, only 150 parties – responsible for three-quarters of global emissions – have submitted new NDCs.

Iran, Vietnam, Egypt and Argentina are among those without new NDCs – and the US has withdrawn its climate plan under the Trump administration.

Some parties, such as the EU, have stressed the need for countries to submit their new NDCs ahead of COP31 – and to ensure they are aligned with the 1.5C temperature limit.

COP31 will also see the launch of the second global stocktake, which will conclude in 2028.

Turkey will be pushin

analysis.tldr: International climate talks at COP31 could eventually shift global funding and trade rules, making green energy cheaper or fossil fuels costlier for India over time.
the_story: Delegates are gathering in Antalya, Turkey, for the UN climate negotiations (COP31), which has a joint presidency of Australia leading talks and Turkey hosting.
Developing countries are pushing rich nations for more climate finance and public funding under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, amid aid budget cuts and US pressure on development banks.
Nations are clashing over the mitigation work programme (cutting greenhouse gas emissions), with disagreements on whether it should continue or end.
Only 150 parties have submitted new national climate plans (NDCs) out to 2035, while nations like Iran, Vietnam, Egypt, Argentina, and the US have not submitted them or have withdrawn.
analysis.what_happened: Governments are meeting in Turkey for the COP31 climate summit to negotiate global rules on cutting emissions, climate adaptation, and financial aid from rich countries to developing ones. These talks are struggling against a backdrop of global wars, energy crises, and deep disagreements over who should pay for the transition to cleaner economies.
analysis.analogy: It is like a group project where everyone agrees the house needs repairs, but nobody wants to pay the contractor or agree on who caused the damage.
why_it_matters_india: Global climate talks debate how much money rich nations must give to developing countries like India for green projects.
Disagreements over cutting fossil fuels (mitigation) could eventually pressure India to shift faster away from coal and oil.
New international rules on green industrialisation could alter the costs of imports and exports for Indian manufacturing.
Changes in global finance flows might alter how easily Indian renewable energy companies get cheap international loans.

impacts.target: Renewable energy stocks like Tata Power, Adani Green, & ReNew
impacts.rationale: Global pressure for green transitions and potential climate finance could open up more funding, which is generally good for clean energy companies.

impacts.target: Traditional fossil fuel and coal-dependent stocks like NTPC or Coal India
impacts.rationale: Strict global emissions targets and calls to transition away from fossil fuels create regulatory headwinds, which can pressure traditional energy businesses.

watch_next: Whether developed nations agree to provide more public climate finance to developing nations
Updates from the mitigation work programme on cutting greenhouse gas emissions
analysis.caveats: The article is an interactive preview tracking negotiating positions, so final binding outcomes and financial pledges at COP31 remain highly uncertain.

analysis.tldr: The government has spent more than it earned in the first six months, which could mean the government might need to borrow more money from the market.
the_story: India's fiscal deficit (the gap between government spending and earnings) hit Rs 7.14 lakh crore for the first half of the financial year through September.
This deficit reached 42.1% of the full-year target set for the financial year 2027.
Total government receipts (money collected) came in at Rs 18.35 lakh crore, which is 50.3% of what was expected for the whole year.
The government's full-year fiscal deficit is budgeted at Rs 16.96 lakh crore.
Major subsidy expenditures (money given by the government to keep essentials affordable) reached roughly Rs 6.55 lakh crore.
analysis.what_happened: The government spent significantly more money than it brought in through taxes and other revenues during the first half of the fiscal year, driven heavily by Rs 6.55 lakh crore spent on subsidies. Because expenses are outpacing income, the fiscal deficit has widened to 42.1% of the annual target.
analysis.analogy: It is like a household spending more on groceries and bills in the first six months than its combined salaries, forcing it to rely more on credit cards or loans to cover the gap.
why_it_matters_india: Government spends more than it earns -> fiscal deficit widens
Government needs to cover the shortfall -> borrows more money by issuing bonds (government debt securities)
Higher government borrowing -> increases bond yield (the interest rate the government pays to borrow)
Higher bond yields -> can push up overall interest rates in the economy, making loans costlier for regular people

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: Higher government borrowing usually pushes yields up, which is generally bad as it can make loans more expensive.
Persistent high deficits can sometimes weigh on the currency, making imports like crude oil costlier for everyday citizens.

watch_next: Government borrowing announcements for the second half of the year
Updates on total tax collections and whether subsidies stay within the budget limit
analysis.caveats: This report only covers the first half of the fiscal year, and government revenues often pick up in the later months.

events.headline: Gold - backed agriculture loans : RBI proposes changes to priority sector lending rules ; what could change for borrowers

items.title: Gold - backed agriculture loans : RBI proposes changes to priority sector lending rules ; what could change for borrowers

events.article_text:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has proposed changes to priority sector lending (PSL) calculations and documentation requirements for banks, with implications for agricultural lending and the treatment of certain trade-credit exposures. The proposals include stricter verification of gold-backed agricultural loans and a change in how banks account for trade bills discounted under letters of credit (LCs) while calculating their priority sector lending obligations. The changes form part of RBI's draft Reserve Bank of India (Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification) Directions, 2026, released on November 5. The central bank has invited comments until November 26. Under the draft, banks will have to maintain details such as the location of land under cultivation, crops grown and hypothecation of crops, wherever applicable. They must also ensure that the sanctioned loan amount is based on the applicable scale of finance and a proper assessment of the credit requirements for the agricultural activity, rather than solely on the type or value of collateral. Banks will additionally have to maintain records of field visits by officials to monitor the end use of loans. For landless agricultural labourers and sharecroppers who do not have land records or lease deeds, banks must maintain alternative verifiable documents to establish their eligibility for PSL classification. However, pledging gold jewellery or ornaments does not automatically disqualify an agricultural loan from PSL benefits. The RBI draft clarifies, “Bank loans extended for agricultural activities do not become ineligible for priority sector classification merely because the underlying collateral is in the form of gold jewellery or ornaments.” Another significant proposal concerns bills purchased, discounted or negotiated by banks under letters of credit. The RBI has proposed that such bills should not be excluded from ‘bank credit in India’ while calculating net bank credit (NBC) and adjusted net bank credit (ANBC) for PSL purposes. Banks can treat these exposures as interbank exposures for the limited purposes of exposure and capital adequacy calculations, but not for excluding them from the PSL calculation. This could increase the base against which banks calculate their priority sector lending obligations. For instance, every additional ₹10,000 crore included in ANBC would translate into an additional PSL requirement of ₹4,000 crore at the existing 40% target for domestic commercial banks. The corresponding agriculture target would increase by ₹1,800 crore, including a ₹1,400 crore sub-target for non-corporate farmers and ₹1,000 crore for small and marginal farmers. The non-corporate farmer and small and marginal farmer targets are nested within the agriculture target and should not be added to it separately. The micro-enterprise and weaker-section targets would also increase by ₹750 crore and ₹1,200 crore, respectively. For agricultural borrowers, particularly farmers pledging gold jewellery, the proposal does not prohibit gold-backed loans from qualifying as PSL. However, banks may seek more supporting documents on cultivation, crops and loan utilisation, potentially making the verification process more rigorous. Disclaimer: The RBI's proposals are part of draft directions and are subject to change following stakeholder feedback. analysis.tldr: Stricter paperwork for gold-backed farm loans and broader lending calculations by the RBI could change how banks hand out priority sector loans.
the_story: On November 5, the RBI (Reserve Bank of India, the country's central banking institution) released draft rules proposing changes to priority sector lending (PSL, loans to sectors like agriculture that the government considers important for the economy).

Under the new rules, banks must strictly verify gold-backed agricultural loans by keeping records of land locations, crops grown, and proof of crop hypothecation (pledging assets as security without handing over possession).
Pledging gold jewellery will not disqualify a farm loan from priority sector benefits, but banks must base loan amounts on actual farming needs rather than just the value of the gold.

The RBI also proposed changing how banks calculate their total lending base by including certain trade bills, which could automatically increase the overall amount banks must lend to priority sectors like agriculture and small businesses.
analysis.what_happened: The Reserve Bank of India issued draft directions to tighten rules around agricultural loans backed by gold and change how banks calculate their mandatory lending targets for priority sectors. The proposed changes require banks to collect much more proof of actual farming activity and proper loan usage instead of just accepting gold as collateral, while also expanding the calculation base for total bank lending.
analysis.analogy: It is like a school checking not just if you brought your notebook to class, but demanding receipts and progress reports to prove you are actually doing the homework inside it.
why_it_matters_india: The RBI changes how banks calculate their total lending base (ANBC [adjusted net bank credit, the total lending base used to calculate mandatory priority sector targets]).
A bigger lending base automatically forces commercial banks to set aside more money for priority sectors like agriculture, micro-enterprises, and weaker sections.
For farmers using gold to secure loans, getting money may require more paperwork, land records, and proof of crop cultivation.
Landless labourers and sharecroppers will need alternative verifiable documents to qualify for these special loans.

impacts.rationale: Stricter paperwork and proof of crop cultivation could slow down or reduce casual gold-backed farm lending, which is good for preventing loan misuse but potentially frustrating for genuine borrowers needing quick cash.

impacts.target: Priority sector lending by commercial banks
impacts.rationale: Including trade bills in the lending base means banks must expand their total priority sector lending targets, potentially increasing credit availability for small businesses and farmers.

watch_next: The final guidelines released by the RBI after public comments close on November 26.
How commercial banks adjust their gold loan verification processes.
analysis.caveats: These are only draft directions released for public feedback and could change before becoming final rules.

events.article_text:

IL JIN Electronics (India) Ltd, an arm of Amber Enterprises India Ltd, has filed preliminary papers with the market regulator Sebi to raise Rs 2,500 crore through an initial public offering (IPO).

The proposed IPO is entirely a fresh issue of equity shares, with no offer for sale (OFS) component, according to the draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) dated November 6.

The company plans to use the proceeds to repay or prepay certain outstanding borrowings, including accrued interest, availed by the company and its subsidiaries, Ascent Circuits and Shogini Technoarts.

IL JIN Electronics is a vertically integrated, technology-driven electronics design and manufacturing company operating across four business verticals -- electronics manufacturing services (EMS), bare printed circuit board (PCB) manufacturing, power electronics and industrial automation.

The company is a subsidiary of Amber Enterprises India Ltd, a major player in India's room air-conditioner original equipment manufacturer (OEM) and original design manufacturer (ODM) industry.

IL JIN Electronics operates 11 manufacturing facilities, including 10 in India and one in Israel. Its Indian facilities are located in Noida and Greater Noida in Uttar Pradesh, Pune in Maharashtra, Chennai and Hosur in Tamil Nadu, and Bengaluru in Karnataka.

Six additional manufacturing facilities are currently under construction and are expected to support its future capacity expansion.

On the financial front, IL JIN Electronics' revenue from operations rose to Rs 3,268.47 crore in FY26 from Rs 1,240.41 crore in FY24. Its EBITDA grew from Rs 321.07 crore in FY26 from Rs 71.42 crore in FY24.

Motilal Oswal Investment Advisors, Axis Capital and Jefferies India have been appointed as the book-running lead managers to the issue, while KFin Technologies will act as the registrar to the IPO.

analysis.tldr: IL JIN Electronics filing to raise ₹2,500 crore shows strong growth in India's electronic manufacturing sector, which can boost confidence in parent company stocks and local manufacturing jobs.
the_story: IL JIN Electronics (India) Ltd, a subsidiary of Amber Enterprises India Ltd, filed preliminary papers (DRHP [Draft Red Herring Prospectus, an official document a company files to give investors details before a share sale]) with Sebi [Securities and Exchange Board of India, the market regulator] to raise ₹2,500 crore through an IPO [Initial Public Offering, when a private company first sells its shares to the public].

The IPO is entirely a fresh issue of equity shares (new shares created by the company), meaning there is no offer for sale (OFS [when existing investors sell their old shares to the public]) component.
The raised funds will be used to clear debts, buy plant, machinery, and equipment for manufacturing units, and for general corporate purposes.

IL JIN Electronics operates 11 manufacturing facilities (10 in India, one in Israel) across four business verticals like electronics manufacturing and PCB [Printed Circuit Board, the green board that connects electronic components] manufacturing, with six more facilities under construction.
The company's revenue from operations rose to ₹3,268.47 crore and EBITDA [Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization, a measure of core operating profit] grew to ₹321.07 crore.
analysis.what_happened: IL JIN Electronics, an electronics manufacturing arm of Amber Enterprises, has officially asked market regulators for permission to launch a ₹2,500 crore IPO. The company plans to use the money it raises to pay off its debts and buy new factory equipment to expand its business.
analysis.analogy: It is like a successful hardware store chain asking the public for money to pay off its debts and build five new mega-stores because customer demand is booming.

The company uses the fresh capital to clear loans and expand factories ->
Increased manufacturing capacity boosts local electronics production and jobs ->
Investor interest grows in Indian manufacturing and EMS [Electronics Manufacturing Services, companies that build electronic parts for other brands] sectors.

impacts.target: Amber Enterprises India Ltd (Parent company stock)
impacts.rationale: A major successful subsidiary expanding and raising funds can improve the parent company's market value, which is generally good for shareholders.
Large capital raises for building factories signal robust growth in domestic production, which is good for the broader economy and jobs.

history.title: The scam that built India's market plumbing
history.what: A journalist revealed that broker Harshad Mehta had been using forged bank receipts to divert money from the interbank government bond market into shares, driving the Sensex up over 140% in a year. When the mechanism was exposed the index fell roughly 40%.
history.why: The bond settlement system relied on paper receipts and personal trust between banks. There was no electronic record, no central depository, and no regulator with real teeth. Shares settled fortnightly, which let a broker build enormous positions with no money down. The fraud was not clever so much as inevitable given the plumbing.
history.impact: About ₹4,000 crore of public bank money was diverted — enormous for the time. Several bank chairmen were arrested. Retail investors who had bought into the boom lost heavily, and Indian equity took years to recover its reputation with ordinary savers.
history.policy: SEBI, which had existed only as an advisory body, was given statutory powers in 1992. The National Stock Exchange was created as an electronic, screen-based competitor to the broker-controlled BSE. Shares were dematerialised into depositories, and physical certificates disappeared.
history.consequence: This is why buying a share in India today is instant, electronic and safe, settled by a central depository with a regulator behind it — infrastructure that many richer countries took longer to build. The scandal's cost bought the market's plumbing.
history.pattern: Financial scandals almost never come from exotic instruments. They come from a settlement gap, a trust-based process, or a regulator without authority. Ask where the paperwork is manual and who checks it.
history.india_echo: The sequel arrived in 2001 with Ketan Parekh, exploiting the remaining carry-forward settlement system; that ended badla trading and brought in rolling settlement. Two scandals, two upgrades — the pattern of Indian market reform.
history.watch_for: Any market where the same institution executes, settles and audits. The crypto exchange failures of 2022 were this exact structure, rediscovered.
